     later use.                                                                                                         
                                                                                                                        
     If the resolver lacks a cached answer, it starts at the root. Root servers know the addresses of the top-level     
     domain (TLD) servers, such as those for .com, .org, or .uk. The root responds with a referral pointing to the      
     relevant TLD server. The resolver then queries that TLD server, which returns a referral to the authoritative      
     name server responsible for the specific domain, for example example.com.                                          
                                                                                                                        
     The resolver finally queries the authoritative name server, which holds the definitive records for that domain.    
     It responds with the requested record, commonly an A record (IPv4 address) or AAAA record (IPv6 address), though   
     many other types exist for mail, aliases, and verification. The resolver returns this answer to your device,       
     which then opens the connection to the destination IP.                                                             
                                                                                                                        
     Caching is central to performance. Answers carry a time-to-live (TTL) value telling resolvers how long they may    
     store the result. Longer TTLs reduce lookup traffic but slow propagation of changes; shorter TTLs do the           
     opposite. Records can also be served through intermediary servers that add resilience, and DNSSEC adds             
     cryptographic signatures so resolvers can verify that answers are authentic and unmodified.                        
                                                                                                                        
     In practice, most lookups finish in milliseconds from cache. A cold, uncached lookup involves several round        
     trips across the hierarchy, which is why caching at every layer, from browser to resolver, matters so much for     
     everyday browsing speed.
